blocks.content: At almost any moment on a running computer, there are more processes that want the CPU than there are CPU cores to give them. Something has to decide which process runs next and for how long. That decision maker is the CPU scheduler, and this module is entirely about how it makes that decision well.

This chapter is the opening topic of the CPU Scheduling module. Before looking at any specific algorithm, it is worth slowing down and asking a more basic question: why does scheduling need to exist at all, what is it actually trying to achieve, and why is there no single perfect answer. Every algorithm covered later in this module, from First Come First Served to Round Robin, is really just a different opinion on how to answer that question.
1. The Core Problem

A modern computer runs many processes at once: a browser, a music player, a code editor, background services, and more. Each of these processes needs the CPU to make progress, but a typical machine has only a handful of CPU cores, often far fewer than the number of processes competing for them. The moment you have more contenders than cores, someone must pick a winner.

That someone is the operating system, and the specific part of it responsible for the choice is called the CPU scheduler. The scheduler looks at every process sitting in the ready queue, meaning every process that is loaded into memory and able to run if given the chance, and decides which one gets the CPU next and for roughly how long.

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: Scheduling exists because CPU demand almost always exceeds CPU supply, and something has to decide who goes first.
It is a resource allocation problem
blocks.text: It is a resource allocation problem

blocks.content: Strip away the operating system language and this is a familiar kind of problem: a scarce resource, many requesters, and a need for a rule that decides allocation. The CPU is the scarce resource, processes are the requesters, and the scheduling algorithm is the rule. The rest of this module explores different rules and what each one optimizes for.
2. Why This Matters for the User
blocks.text: 2. Why This Matters for the User

blocks.content: It is tempting to think of scheduling as an internal bookkeeping detail, but it directly shapes what using a computer feels like. Imagine, for a moment, that there was no scheduler at all, and whichever process happened to start running simply kept the CPU until it finished on its own.

Under that scheme, one long running process, say a video export or a large file compression, could occupy the CPU for minutes or hours at a stretch. Every other process, including the one responding to your mouse clicks and keyboard input, would sit untouched in the ready queue the entire time. The system would feel completely frozen, even though it is technically still working.
Without a scheduler actively making decisions, one greedy process can monopolize the CPU forever, and every other process starves in silence.

Good scheduling is what prevents this. It interrupts long running processes at reasonable intervals, gives short interactive tasks a chance to run quickly, and creates the illusion that many programs are progressing at once even on a machine with only a few cores. When scheduling works well, you rarely notice it. When it works badly, the entire machine feels sluggish or unresponsive, even if no individual process is broken.
3. Goals a Good Scheduler Tries to Balance
blocks.text: 3. Goals a Good Scheduler Tries to Balance

blocks.content: A scheduler is not judged by one single measurement. It is judged against a handful of goals at the same time, and different algorithms lean toward different goals. The table below lists the goals that come up again and again in this module.

{"headers":["Goal","What it means"],"rows":[["Maximize CPU utilization","Keep the CPU as busy as possible instead of sitting idle while work is available."],["Maximize throughput","Complete as many processes as possible per unit of time."],["Minimize turnaround time","Reduce the total time from a process arrival until its completion."],["Minimize waiting time","Reduce the total time a process spends sitting in the ready queue without running."],["Minimize response time","Reduce the time from a request until the first response, which matters most for interactive systems."]]}

blocks.title: CPU utilization and throughput
blocks.content: These two describe how well the system as a whole is performing. A busy CPU that completes more work per second is good for the system.

blocks.title: Turnaround, waiting and response time
blocks.content: These three describe the experience of a single process. A short wait and a fast first response are what make a system feel alive to a user.
4. Why These Goals Genuinely Conflict

If all five goals could be satisfied at once, there would be no need for this module; one algorithm would win and the discussion would end there. In reality, these goals pull against each other, and a scheduler must trade one off for another.

["Favoring short jobs improves average turnaround time, since most processes finish quickly, but it can starve long jobs indefinitely if short jobs keep arriving and keep jumping ahead of them.","Favoring strict fairness, where every process gets an equal, predictable share of the CPU, can hurt overall throughput, since constant switching between processes adds overhead and slows the system down.","Favoring fast response time for interactive processes can increase the waiting time of background processes that are just as important to finish eventually.","Maximizing CPU utilization by never letting the CPU sit idle can conflict with minimizing response time, since the CPU may be busy with a low priority task exactly when a high priority one arrives."]
items: Favoring short jobs improves average turnaround time, since most processes finish quickly, but it can starve long jobs indefinitely if short jobs keep arriving and keep jumping ahead of them.

Favoring strict fairness, where every process gets an equal, predictable share of the CPU, can hurt overall throughput, since constant switching between processes adds overhead and slows the system down.
Favoring fast response time for interactive processes can increase the waiting time of background processes that are just as important to finish eventually.
Maximizing CPU utilization by never letting the CPU sit idle can conflict with minimizing response time, since the CPU may be busy with a low priority task exactly when a high priority one arrives.

blocks.content: This is the central lesson of this entire chapter: there is no single scheduling algorithm that is best at everything. A scheduler that is excellent for average turnaround time may be unfair to long processes. A scheduler that is perfectly fair may waste time switching between processes and lower throughput. Every design is a set of tradeoffs made on purpose.

blocks.title: Why this module has several algorithms
blocks.content: FCFS, SJF and SRTF, Priority Scheduling, and Round Robin each represent a different philosophy about which goals matter most. None of them is objectively correct. Each is the right choice for a different kind of workload.
5. One CPU, Many Processes

The picture below captures the core problem in one image. Several processes sit in the ready queue at the same time, all wanting to run, but only one of them can actually be on the CPU at any given instant. The scheduler is the gate that decides who passes through and in what order.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408415711-30384729.png

Every algorithm in this module is really just a different rule for how that gate operates. Some open it in the order processes arrived. Some let the shortest job go first. Some use priority labels. Some give everyone a small fixed slice and cycle around. The gate itself never changes; only the rule behind it does.
6. A Worked Example

Consider three processes that all arrive at nearly the same moment, all wanting the CPU right away. Call them P1, P2, and P3. Without a scheduler making a deliberate choice, the order in which they run would essentially be arbitrary, or it would default to whichever process happened to be seen first, which is really just First Come First Served by accident rather than by design.
{"headers":["Process","Arrival time","Burst time (time needed on CPU)"],"rows":[["P1","0","10 ms"],["P2","0","2 ms"],["P3","0","4 ms"]]}

If the scheduler simply runs P1 first because it happened to arrive first, P2 and P3 both wait behind a long process even though they need very little CPU time each. If instead the scheduler always picks the shortest remaining job first, P2 finishes almost immediately, P3 follows shortly after, and P1 runs last, which lowers the average waiting time across all three processes even though P1 personally waits longer than before.

Neither answer is universally right. The first treats every process as equally deserving of a turn in arrival order. The second favors overall efficiency at the cost of making the longer process wait. As this module walks through FCFS, SJF and SRTF, Priority Scheduling, and Round Robin, it will return to examples exactly like this one and show how each algorithm handles the same set of processes very differently.
7. When Scheduling Decisions Get Made

A scheduling decision is not something that happens continuously; it happens at specific moments when a process changes state. Broadly, these moments are when a process switches from running to waiting, for example because it needs to perform input or output, when a process switches from running to ready, for example because its time slice expired, when a process switches from waiting to ready, for example because the input or output it was waiting for has completed, and when a process terminates.

Whether the scheduler is allowed to step in at every one of these moments, or only at some of them, defines whether a scheduling scheme is preemptive or non preemptive. That distinction is important enough that it gets its own dedicated topic later in this module, the sibling chapter on Preemptive vs Non Preemptive Scheduling. For now, it is enough to know that scheduling decisions are tied to these state changes rather than happening at random.
8. What This Module Covers Next

With the core problem and the competing goals now in view, the rest of this module walks through the major scheduling algorithms one at a time, showing how each one balances utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, and response time differently.

["First Come First Served, the simplest possible rule, where processes run strictly in arrival order.","Shortest Job First and Shortest Remaining Time First, which prioritize short work to reduce average waiting and turnaround time.","Priority Scheduling, which lets processes carry an explicit priority label that decides who runs next.","Round Robin, which gives every process a small fixed slice of the CPU and cycles through the ready queue, favoring fairness and responsiveness."]
items: First Come First Served, the simplest possible rule, where processes run strictly in arrival order.
Shortest Job First and Shortest Remaining Time First, which prioritize short work to reduce average waiting and turnaround time.
Priority Scheduling, which lets processes carry an explicit priority label that decides who runs next.
Round Robin, which gives every process a small fixed slice of the CPU and cycles through the ready queue, favoring fairness and responsiveness.

blocks.content: Each of these algorithms will be measured against the same goals introduced in this chapter, and each will be shown to be strong in some situations and weak in others. That is the whole point of studying more than one. By the end of the module, the tradeoffs discussed here in the abstract will feel concrete and familiar.
